description: 'Which should I learn?' guide for an English-speaking learner in the US or Canada. Written to inform, not to rank traditions. The evidence on what American congregations actually do is thin: one published survey measured one or two words. Every entry says so and tells the learner to check their own congregation.
evidenceNote: The only quantitative source read is Benor and Cohen's survey (BJPA). It asked which form of 'Festival of Booths' people use; 'soo-COAT' (Israeli) was chosen by 68% of Reform, 73% of Conservative, 70% of Modern Orthodox, 50% of Orthodox and 38% of Black Hat respondents, 'SUK-kiss' (Ashkenazic) by 34, 34, 47, 67 and 73% (people could pick both, so rows add to more than 100). Self-reported, snowball sample, not representative, one word. It tells you tendencies, not what your synagogue does. The survey asked Jews in the United States; Canadian congregations were not measured.
universalAdvice: Ask the people you will pray with. Listen to a service or a recording from your own congregation before you choose.
Practice varies inside a single synagogue: the cantor, the rabbi, older members and the Torah reader may each say things differently.
Chabad.org's own article says all dialects of Hebrew are acceptable; it is a matter of community custom, not of right and wrong.

If you are unsure, learn the Israeli-based sounds first. They are what the Hebrew of Israel uses and what most non-Orthodox respondents in the survey reported, and the Ashkenazi switches (tav, kamatz, cholam, tsere, stress) can be added afterwards.

situations.title: A Reform synagogue in the US or Canada
situations.summary: Most likely Israeli-based sounds, which the app calls the American-synagogue setting. Expect some Ashkenazi forms in familiar words and songs.
caveats: In the survey, Reform respondents were the group most likely to choose the Israeli form of the one word asked about, but about a third also use the Ashkenazic form.
Individual cantors and older members often keep Ashkenazi habits.
situations.askFirst: Which pronunciation do the cantor and the Torah readers use, and is there a recording I can practise with?

situations.title: A Conservative synagogue in the US or Canada
situations.summary: Again, Israeli-based sounds are the more common choice in the survey, with a large Ashkenazic minority. Congregations differ.
caveats: One word measured: 73% chose the Israeli form, 34% the Ashkenazic form.
Congregations differ, and the survey cannot tell you which kind yours is.
situations.askFirst: Does the shul use Israeli-style pronunciation for Torah reading and for the siddur, or does it differ between the two?

situations.title: A Modern Orthodox synagogue in the US or Canada
situations.summary: Mixed. The survey found both forms common (70% Israeli, 47% Ashkenazic for the one word). Listen first.
caveats: Many Modern Orthodox people switch between forms depending on setting.
Torah reading and prayer may use a different pronunciation from everyday Hebrew words.
situations.askFirst: What do the rabbi and the baal koreh (Torah reader) use?

situations.title: An Orthodox or Haredi synagogue in the US or Canada
situations.summary: Ashkenazi pronunciation is more common here than elsewhere in the survey, but not universal. Half of the Orthodox respondents also reported the Israeli form, so Israeli-style and Sephardi communities exist inside Orthodoxy too.
caveats: Survey: 67% (Orthodox) and 73% (Black Hat) chose the Ashkenazic form of the one word, yet 50% and 38% chose the Israeli form.
Ashkenazi has regional dialects. Aleph models one common siddur style; your community's may differ (for example oy or ey for cholam).
situations.askFirst: Which dialect of Ashkenazi does my community use, and who can I copy?

situations.title: A Sephardi, Mizrahi or other non-Ashkenazi community
situations.summary: The app's Sephardi-values setting matches the vowels (a, e, i, o, u) but not your community's consonants, which may include pharyngeal het and ayin.
caveats: 'Sephardi' covers many communities with different habits (Spanish-Portuguese, North African, Balkan, Levantine, Iraqi, Yemenite and more).
Aleph does not model any of them in detail. Use it for reading practice and take the sounds from a member of your community.
situations.askFirst: Can someone from my community record or sit with me for the throat sounds and for how they say the prayers?

situations.title: Preparing to read Torah or lead prayers (for example for a bar or bat mitzvah)
situations.summary: Use the tradition your synagogue and teacher use. That choice is made by your community, not by this app.
caveats: Cantillation (the trope melodies) is a separate topic not taught here.
Take the recording or the teacher's reading as the final authority for your congregation.
situations.askFirst: Which pronunciation and which melodies does my teacher expect?

situations.title: Travelling or living in Israel
situations.summary: Learn the Modern Israeli sounds. Everyday Israeli Hebrew has no pharyngeals for most speakers, a back-of-the-throat r, and mostly final stress.
caveats: Some older Mizrahi Israelis still use pharyngeal sounds, and Israeli synagogues keep Ashkenazi, Sephardi, Mizrahi and Yemenite customs side by side.
Aleph does not teach Tel Aviv slang or informal fast speech: no source for those was found.
situations.askFirst: Is it for travel talk (Israeli track) or for services in Israel (ask the synagogue)?

background.title: Why does Israeli Hebrew sound Sephardi? A short story for beginners
paragraphs: Hebrew letters have been spelled the same way for two thousand years, but Jews in different countries said them differently. Jews in Spain, North Africa and the Middle East (Sephardim) kept one set of sounds; Jews in Germany and Eastern Europe (Ashkenazim) kept another. The famous test: the vowel kamatz is ah for Sephardim and o for Ashkenazim, so the same word is Shabbat for one and Shabbos for the other, and the letter tav without a dot is t for one and s for the other.

Around 1900, when people started speaking Hebrew every day again in the land of Israel, almost all of them had grown up with the Ashkenazi sounds. They chose the Sephardi sounds anyway. Why? The old Jewish community of Jerusalem was Sephardi and was respected; Eliezer Ben-Yehuda and the first Hebrew teachers worked with them; the Bible's own stress marks put the accent at the end of most words, which is how Sephardim read; and the new settlers wanted a sound that was not the sound of the European villages they had left behind.

In 1903 the Hebrew teachers' assembly in Palestine made it official: the new schools would teach the Sephardi pronunciation. Children learned it; their parents mostly did not. Writers who arrived later, such as the novelist Agnon, kept an Ashkenazi tinge all their lives, and old kibbutz members could still be heard stressing words the Ashkenazi way.

The new Israeli accent took the Sephardi vowels and stress, but it was spoken by European mouths. Two Sephardi sounds did not survive the move: the throaty ayin and the throaty chet. Most Israelis today say ayin as a silent letter and chet like the kh in khaf, and they say resh at the back of the throat, where Sephardim roll it at the front. That is why this app has three settings and not two: Modern Israeli is the Sephardi system without the throat sounds.

What this means for you: if you will read in a Reform or Conservative synagogue in North America, the Israeli-style sounds are what you will hear most, with a few Ashkenazi words kept by habit. If your community is Sephardi or Mizrahi, add the throat sounds for ayin and chet and roll the r. If it is Orthodox Ashkenazi, expect Shabbos, Borukh and oy-sounds. None of these is wrong; each is a community's way of reading the same letters.
background.note: Written for Aleph from the sources listed; no sentence was copied. History simplified for beginners; the full account is Harshav, chapter 27.
